source.title: ECG-InterpBench: Benchmarking the Interpretability of ECG Foundation Models with Matched-Scale Sparse Autoencoders

page_placements.theme: Widening can give little benefit or worsen reconstruction

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures SAE reconstruction fidelity across dictionary scales, but does not analyze residual vectors for linear predictability, per-token error-norm scaling, or overlap of failure contexts. Its SAE reconstruction results do not directly test the claim versions as stated.
record.gate_note: The paper reports reconstruction-fidelity outcomes across SAE scales and models; these are recorded as findings about aggregate reconstruction fidelity, not as tests of dark-matter structure. Other reported outcomes, including clinical accessibility, random-coordinate calibration, and SAE-versus-dense interventions, do not measure the claim versions. The paper cites prior SAE work but reports no dark-matter-specific results.
record.test_reason: An ECG foundation-model interpretability benchmark. It reports only aggregate BatchTopK SAE reconstruction R² and AUC across widths, depths and models. It never analyses the error vector's linear predictability, per-token error norms, failure-context overlap, loss effects of splicing or error-term function, and it does not cite the dark-matter paper. Flat R² near 0.95–0.97 under a fixed k=96 budget is a different construct from V2's per-token predictability claim. It also cannot isolate whether error persists with scale, because active features stay fixed as width grows.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that ECG FMs have distinct, metric-specific interpretability profiles: reconstruction fidelity, single-coordinate clinical accessibility and cross-seed reproducibility identify different leaders. The profiles replicate on MIMIC-IV-ECG. They draw no conclusions about the structure or function of SAE error.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains matched-scale BatchTopK SAEs on frozen ECG foundation-model activations and reports aggregate reconstruction fidelity alongside clinical and reproducibility metrics; it does not perform the original dark-matter residual analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: Reconstruction fidelity varies with expansion factor, model, depth, and cohort; the authors also report differences under fixed-k/d versus fixed-k/N sparsity parameterizations.

fits_no_version.finding: Under fixed k=96, aggregate PTB-XL validation R² is 0.968, 0.953, 0.949, 0.947 and 0.948 for E=1–32, so it is non-monotonic in width. Dead-feature fraction rises from 0.019 to 0.604.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For ECG foundation-model activations at a fixed active budget, widening a BatchTopK SAE does not reduce aggregate reconstruction error and mostly adds dead latents.

fits_no_version.finding: On MIMIC-IV-ECG, aggregate R² stays at 0.970–0.973 across E. Model-level reconstruction AUC differs across encoders (0.916–0.990) with a stable ordering (Kendall tau 1.00).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE reconstruction fidelity is a stable, encoder-specific property of ECG representations across dictionary widths and cohorts.

record.problems: The reported fidelity measures are aggregate reconstruction metrics and do not resolve the claim's per-token error structure, linear predictability, or overlap of failed contexts. Some reported scale summaries average across models, depths, and SAE seeds.
record.rows_left_out: No other reconstruction-fidelity values relevant to the claim were omitted. Clinical accessibility, random-coordinate comparisons, and SAE-versus-dense intervention results were left out because they do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No regression of SAE error on input activations.

No per-token error-norm prediction and no overlap of failing contexts across sizes. Aggregate R² vs width is reported only at fixed k, so whether error vanishes with scale is not tested in the claim's sense.
No splicing of reconstructions into the model and no loss comparison against random errors of matched size.
No decomposition of error into linear and nonlinear parts.
No circuit or steering analysis comparing results with and without the error term. The SAE-vs-dense intervention selectivity (Appendix G) does not measure error-term contribution.
No test of whether residual error is a training artifact. The fixed-k/N arm changes reconstruction AUC by -0.012 to -0.042 but does not analyse dark matter.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation 'discusses' is changed to 'cites_only' as the nearest option. The paper neither cites nor discusses the dark-matter claim. Its SAE reconstruction results are aggregate fidelity metrics used for model comparison. All rows correctly carry versions ['none'].

versions.untested_parts: No analysis of whether SAE error vectors are linearly predictable from input activations.
No per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, no analysis of whether different SAE sizes fail on the same contexts, and no direct test of the stated error-scaling claim.
No replacement of model activations by SAE reconstructions followed by comparison with matched-size random errors on model loss.
No decomposition of SAE error into linear and nonlinear components, nor test of their feature-learning properties.
No test of whether circuits, steering, or other SAE-feature analyses lose model behavior when the error term is omitted.
No test of whether dark matter is chiefly an SAE-training artifact or whether improved architectures or end-to-end training reduce it.

relation.reason: The text discusses reconstruction limitations across dictionary widths, but contains no identifiable citation to the dark-matter finding. Its cited SAE literature provides general background on scaling and evaluation.

tranche.reason: Aggregate reconstruction fidelity and dictionary utilization do not test any claim version. The study neither characterizes SAE residual structure nor uses a dark-matter finding as a tool.

source_check.notes: The reported R² values are descriptive aggregates, not evidence about per-token error predictability or shared failure contexts. Appendix D explicitly fixes k=96; the authors' metric-specific interpretability conclusion is consistent with the text.
